lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 3 you met nouns and verbs. In "Birds sing", which word is the verb? Sing: it says what the birds do.
A complete sentence has a subject (who or what) and a verb (what they do or are). It makes sense on its own: The buddy jumped.
A fragment is only part of a sentence: Under the big bridge. (Who? Did what?) Fix it: The troll slept under the big bridge.
A run-on joins two sentences with no full stop and no joining word: I found a gem I gave it to Nan. Fix it: I found a gem. I gave it to Nan.
You can also fix a run-on with a comma and a joining word: I found a gem, and I gave it to Nan.
Try it in the world: write one complete sentence on a sign for your house. For example: Our buddy guards the door. Does yours have a subject and a verb? Next: verbs and their -ing tenses.

exercises.prompt: Which is a complete sentence?
exercises.hint: It needs a who and a did-what.
choices: The cat slept on the rug.
exercises.explain: "The cat slept on the rug" has a subject (the cat) and a verb (slept).

exercises.prompt: "Behind the old barn." is a complete sentence.
exercises.hint: Who? Did what?
exercises.explain: No: it is a fragment. It has no subject and no verb.

exercises.prompt: Every complete sentence needs a subject and a…
exercises.hint: Think of "The buddy jumped". Which word tells what the buddy did?
exercises.explain: A sentence needs a subject and a verb.

exercises.prompt: Which is a fragment?
exercises.hint: Which one leaves you waiting for more?
exercises.explain: "Because it was cold" does not make sense on its own.

exercises.prompt: "Birds sing." is a complete sentence.
exercises.hint: Who? Birds. Do what? Sing.
exercises.explain: Yes: a subject and a verb, and it makes sense.

exercises.prompt: Which is a run-on sentence?
exercises.hint: Two sentences squashed together with nothing between them.
choices: The bell rang we ran outside.
The bell rang, so we ran outside.
exercises.explain: "The bell rang we ran outside" joins two sentences with nothing between them.

exercises.prompt: How can you fix the fragment "The tallest tower"?
exercises.hint: Add what the tower did or had.
choices: The tallest tower had a flag.
exercises.explain: Adding a verb (had) makes a complete sentence.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best fix for: "I like apples my brother likes pears."
exercises.hint: Use a comma and a joining word.
choices: I like apples, but my brother likes pears.
I like apples my brother, likes pears.
I like apples. my brother likes pears.
exercises.explain: A comma and "but" join the two sentences correctly.

exercises.prompt: "We built a raft it floated." is a run-on sentence.
exercises.hint: Is it two sentences?
exercises.explain: Yes: "We built a raft" and "It floated" need a full stop, or a comma and a joining word.

exercises.prompt: What is missing from "Ran all the way home."?
exercises.hint: We know what happened. Who did it?
exercises.explain: It has a verb (ran) but no subject: who ran?

exercises.prompt: Which is complete and correct?
exercises.hint: One is a run-on and one is a fragment.
choices: It rained, so we played inside.
exercises.explain: A comma and "so" join the two sentences correctly.

exercises.prompt: Which group of words is NOT a complete sentence?
exercises.hint: Which one needs more to make sense?
exercises.explain: "When the sun went down" leaves you asking: what happened? Add a main part to finish it: When the sun went down, the owls woke up.

exercises.prompt: "The fox, which was hungry." is a complete sentence.
exercises.hint: What did the fox do?
exercises.explain: No: we know about the fox, but not what it did. It needs a verb: The fox, which was hungry, ate.

exercises.prompt: Fix the run-on: "The storm ended the sky turned blue."
exercises.hint: Where does the first sentence stop?
choices: The storm ended. The sky turned blue.
The storm ended the sky. Turned blue.
The storm, ended the sky turned blue.
exercises.explain: "The storm ended" is one sentence; "The sky turned blue" is another.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to make a complete sentence.
exercises.hint: Start with the subject.
exercises.explain: The buddy (subject) carried (verb) a lantern.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: complete sentence, fragment or run-on?
exercises.hint: Is there a subject and a verb? Is there one sentence, or two squashed together?
exercises.explain: Birds sing and the fox ran home are sentences. Under the bridge and because it was late are fragments. It rained we stayed in and I won I was happy are run-ons.

exercises.prompt: Subject or verb?
exercises.hint: Who or what is it about, and what do they do?
exercises.explain: The buddy and a troll are subjects; jumped and slept are verbs.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to what it means.
matches: has a subject and a verb
exercises.hint: A fragment is missing something.
exercises.explain: A fragment is only part of a sentence, a run-on joins two with no full stop, and a complete sentence has a subject and a verb.

exercises.prompt: How many sentences are in this? I found a gem. I gave it to Nan.
exercises.hint: Count the full stops.
exercises.explain: Two sentences: each ends with a full stop.

exercises.prompt: Each one is not a complete sentence. Match it to the fix it needs.
items: I found a gem I gave it to Nan.
exercises.hint: Is a subject missing, a verb, or both? Or are two sentences joined with nothing?
exercises.explain: Under the big bridge has no subject or verb: The troll slept under the big bridge. The gem one is a run-on: I found a gem. I gave it to Nan. Ran all the way home needs a subject: Tam ran all the way home.
